text:
Scarlett was sitting on her bed during quiet time. The house was very still. Then her tummy made a loud noise. Grrrrr! She heard it growl again. It was empty, and it squeezed inside her.

Scarlett went to find Mommy in the kitchen. Mommy was stirring soup on the stove. "My tummy is growling," Scarlett said. "It is empty and noisy." Mommy smiled. "Dinner is almost ready," she said. Scarlett waited on her chair. She did not touch the hot stove.

The soup steamed and bubbled. Mommy poured some into a cool bowl for Scarlett. "The pot is hot, the bowl is just right," Mommy said. Scarlett blew on her spoon, then took a bite. Her tummy rumbled one more time, then went quiet.

Cooper wanted to send a picture to Grandma. He drew a big yellow sun on the paper. His big sister Mia drew a little red flower too. They put the paper in an envelope. Cooper tried to seal it shut. Mia said they could take turns licking it. Cooper licked first, then Mia. Then they wrote Grandma's name on the front.

But Cooper forgot to write where Grandma lives. Mia said the mail carrier needs the address. Mom helped them copy it from a card. Cooper walked outside with Mom. The street was quiet and a little wet from morning rain. Cooper stood on his toes. He let the letter slip into the mailbox. "Now the mail carrier will pick it up," Mom said.

Cooper watched the mailbox for a long time. "It goes to a big building first," Mom said. "Then it comes to Grandma's house." Cooper smiled. A few days later, Grandma called. "I got your sun and flower," she said. Cooper ran to tell Mia. They began drawing a new picture right away.

Livia walked with Mommy through the art gallery. The walls had big paintings of red, yellow and blue. "Can you name the colours?" Mommy asked. "Red! Yellow! Blue!" Livia said. At a table, a man in a smock was mixing paints. He let Livia stir a little cup. Red swirled into blue. "Look!" Livia said. "Red and blue make purple!" Mommy smiled and helped her hold the cup steady.

Then Livia smelled bread from the little café in the corner. A baker had dough in a big bowl. It grew bigger and bigger. "Is it alive?" Livia asked. "It moves because tiny living things inside are eating the sugar and making bubbles," the baker said. "I chased the bubbles away once by squishing the dough, and it started again." "Yucky?" Livia asked. "No, it makes bread yummy," he said, tapping the warm loaf.

Livia held up her purple fingers. "I made a new colour," she said. The baker gave her a small piece of bread. "Thank you," Livia said, and she took a big bite.

Amelia went to the library with her mother. She wanted a book about bunnies. She saw a book with a rabbit on the front. "Books start at the front," her mother said. "We read to the last page." Amelia turned one page at a time. The rabbit in the book had long, long teeth. It was chewing a big leaf.

The story in the book said the rabbit only got cake. The rabbit did not chew grass. Its front teeth grew longer and longer. Amelia turned another page. The rabbit tried to eat grass again. Crunch, crunch, crunch. Its teeth wore down. Soon they were just right.

"Grass helps the bunny," Amelia said. "Chewing plants makes the teeth go down." She read to the very last page. The rabbit munched leaves in the sun.

Amelia waved the book in the air. "I want this one!" she said. Her mother smiled and they went to the desk. The rabbit on the front seemed to smile too.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She saw red tomatoes with her eyes. She smelled warm soup with her nose. Daddy tapped the table. Tap, tap, tap. Aubrey heard it with her ears. She put her hand flat on the table. One finger, two fingers, three. The table wiggled under her hand. Aubrey smiled. "The table is wiggling air," she said. "The wiggles go to my eardrum and make it shake. That is how I hear." Daddy tapped again. Tap, tap, tap, tap. Aubrey felt the table with her hand. Then she heard the taps with her ears. Her problem was solved. She was lucky to have such a good dinner. She tasted the soup with her tongue. Yum.

Nora wanted to zip her red coat all by herself. "First the zipper goes in," said Mom. "Then up, up, up." Nora pushed and pulled. One, two, three little tugs. The zipper slid up! "I did it," Nora said.

Nora heard a loud whoosh from the bathroom. She ran to look. Her toy sheep, Floppy, sat on the floor. Nora pushed the handle. The water rushed from the tank into the bowl. Down the pipe it went. She pushed again. Whoosh! Down, down, down it went.

"I zipped my coat, and the water goes down the pipe," Nora said. She hugged Floppy close. Then she zipped her coat up once more. Up, up, up went the zipper.

Sara went to the library with Mommy. She saw a boy named Leo at the story table. Leo had a scab on his knee. He picked at it with his finger. "Ouch," he said. He looked sad.

Sara sat next to him. "Do not peel it," she said. "The scab is a little lid. New skin grows under the lid." Leo stopped picking. He smiled a happy smile. "I want to see the new skin," he said.

The librarian read a wild story about a bear. Leo and Sara laughed and got excited. Then it was time to go. Mommy said the little store next door had bandages. Sara helped Leo pick a soft one for his knee. "Thank you," Leo said. He put the bandage on and jumped up. "I am all better!" The new skin was growing under the lid.

Yesterday, Declan saw a cloud in the sky. He wanted to touch it. But the cloud was too high up. "How can I touch a cloud?" he asked. "Maybe tomorrow," said his teacher, Miss Amy.

Today, white fog covered the playground. It felt soft and wet on Declan's hands. It tickled his nose. Everything looked different in the fog. Declan walked and walked. The fog stuck to his arms like little drops of water. "Wait," said Declan. "Fog is a cloud on the ground. I am walking in a cloud right now!" He waved his hands in the fog. The problem was solved. He was touching a cloud at last.

Later, the sun came out. The fog went away. "We can play in a cloud again another day," said Miss Amy. Declan smiled and reached up high.

Alice went to the store with her mom. She was very hungry. Mom bought six little cookies. Alice ran to her friend Ben and her friend Sam. "Can I try to share these?" she asked. But Ben and Sam were arguing. "I want more cookies," said Ben. "No, I want more," said Sam. Alice had an idea. "Let's count them out," she said. She gave one cookie to Ben. She gave one cookie to Sam. She counted, "Two, three, four." Then she gave one more to Ben and one more to Sam. Ben had three cookies. Sam had three cookies. "It is fair!" said Sam. Ben smiled too. Alice held her own three cookies. They all sat on the store bench and munched them up.

Charlie stood on a stool in the kitchen. She wanted to butter her own toast today. The butter was cold and hard.

"Can I spread it?" she asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Push gently."

Charlie pushed. The toast tore a little. "Oh," said Charlie. "It tore because I pushed too hard." She pushed softly now. The butter went smooth, all the way to the edge.

Next she poured milk. The cup had a thin blue line inside. "Fill it to the thin line," said Mom. Charlie poured slowly. One, two, three, she counted. The milk stayed in the cup. "I did it!"

Then Sam and Joe came in, arguing over six cookies. "Mine!" said Sam. "Mine!" said Joe. Charlie looked at the plate. "How can we fix it?" she asked. Then she answered herself, "We count!" She put one cookie in front of Sam. One for Joe. Two for Sam. Two for Joe. Three for Sam. Three for Joe.

The plate was empty. "Sam has three, Joe has three," said Charlie. Sam smiled. Joe smiled. Charlie raised her cup of milk.

Maria was playing in the backyard. The sun was big and warm. Maria felt water on her face. "I'm wet!" she said. "Is something wrong?" Mommy was watering flowers nearby. "Come wipe your face," Mommy said, holding a soft cloth. Maria wiped her face. But soon it was wet again. "I'm wet again," Maria said. She wiped and wiped. "Wet again, wet again!" Then Maria sat in the shade. The water dried all by itself. Maria felt cool. "The water dries and I feel cool!" she said. "My skin lets the water out." Mommy smiled. "Look, my new hat keeps the sun off me," Mommy said. "Stay close to me so we can both stay cool." "I will stay close," said Maria. Maria put on her new hat. She sat close by Mommy and watched the flowers.

Madeline was turning four today. Grandma's house smelled like cake. Balloons bobbed by the window. Madeline wanted a new blue balloon for her party.

"Grandpa, can we get one?" she asked. Grandpa took her hand. They walked to the little store on the corner. The store was cool and quiet inside.

Madeline saw the balloon. She gave the man her smile. He did not give it to her. Madeline frowned.

"He needs money," Grandpa said. He gave the man some coins. The man smiled back and handed her the balloon. "The store uses money to buy more things to sell," Grandpa said. "And to pay the workers."

Madeline held the string tight. "Money gets things," she said. "Then the store gets more things!"

"That's right," Grandpa laughed. They walked home in the warm sun. Grandma waved from the porch. She had a chair waiting for Grandpa, and he sat down with a happy sigh.

Madeline ran inside with her balloon. Everyone sang the birthday song. She squeezed her eyes shut and blew out the candles.

Lydia sat with Daddy in the big stadium. The crowd cheered. The players ran fast. Lydia had a scab on her knee from a fall last week. She wanted to peel it off and see what was under it. "No, no," said Daddy. "The scab is a little lid. New skin grows under it." Lydia waited and watched the game instead. One player, two players, three players ran past. "Run, run, run!" she shouted. Her tummy felt jumpy and excited. At the last minute of the game, a player scored a goal. Everyone jumped up. Lydia jumped too. Later at home, she skipped down the hall. She looked at her knee. New pink skin was peeking out. "I waited, and it grew, and it grew," she sang. Lydia skipped one more skip and smiled.

Chloe sat in the kitchen with her rabbit, Pip. "Let's play the senses game!" said Mom. "What do your eyes do?" Chloe looked at a cookie. "Eyes see!" she said. "What do your ears do?" Pip's ears wiggled. "Ears hear!" said Chloe. Her nose smelled the cookie. "Nose smells!" Her tongue licked a crumb. "Tongue tastes!" Her back leaned on the chair. Her hands touched her tummy. "Hands touch!"

Pip hopped up and nibbled the cookie. Then he stopped eating. "Pip, your teeth are so long!" said Chloe. Mom said, "Rabbits eat grass, leaves, and other plants. Their front teeth never stop growing, so they chew tough plants to wear the teeth down." Chloe got crunchy grass and crunchy leaves. Pip chewed and chewed. "He won't stop!" Chloe laughed. Pip's teeth looked just right, and he nibbled her toe to say thank you.

Emilia sat in the line at the clinic. She counted the chairs with her eyes. One, two, three. Soon it would be her turn for a shot.

At the next table, a nurse was cutting an onion for her lunch. Dad stood close and rubbed his eyes. "Are you crying?" Emilia asked. Then she looked at the onion. "No! The onion is making your eyes leak!" she said. Her tears came because of the gas, not because Dad was sad.

"Your turn, Emilia," called the nurse. Emilia felt a little weak in her legs. But Dad held her hand. "See? My eyes stopped stinging," Dad said. The shot was quick, like a mosquito. Emilia counted to three, and it was done. "I want a sticker," she said, jumping up.

It was a stormy morning, so Chloe stayed inside with Mama. Chloe wanted to make her own snack. She spread butter on her toast, but the knife slipped and made a big blob. "Oops!" said Chloe. She pushed slower, and the butter went smooth. Then she poured milk into her little cup. It did not spill one drop.

Next Chloe put crackers on her plate. Some were triangles. Some were squares. The square crackers kept standing up like little walls on the plate. Chloe counted the sides of a square cracker. One, two, three, four. She counted the sides of a triangle. One, two, three. "Squares have four. Triangles have three," said Chloe.

Mama tried to sneak a square cracker. Chloe counted its sides out loud. One, two, three, four. "That is a square," said Chloe, and she fed it right to Mama.

Andrew was learning to swim. His teacher showed him how to kick. Kick, kick, splash. He tried it at the pool every day. One boy was shy and sat by the steps. Andrew waited and waited. Soon the shy boy kicked too.

Then Andrew went to the lake with Daddy. He put his ears in the water. Daddy hummed under the water. The water wiggled. Andrew felt the wiggles in his ear. A tiny skin inside his ear shook. That was how he heard Daddy!

"The water wiggles my ear, and then I hear you!" said Andrew.

"Yes," said Daddy. "Sound is air wiggling. The wiggles make your eardrum shake."

Andrew hummed back. Daddy heard him. "It popped right through the water to me!" said Daddy.

Then Andrew kicked. Kick, kick, splash. After swimming, he took a nap on the warm sand.

Emilia was at the store with Mommy. She saw a mailbox by the door. Emilia had a picture for Grandma. "I want to mail this present picture," she said. She dropped it in the mailbox.

A mail carrier came and opened the box. He looked at Emilia's picture. "There is no address on it," he said. "Where does Grandma live?" Emilia helped Mommy write the address on the front. The mail carrier put it in his big bag.

"It goes to a big building first," he said. "Then it goes to Grandma's house." "Because the address tells where," Emilia said. Mommy held her hand at the counter. They took turns buying apples and bread. Emilia waved at the mail carrier as he walked away.

Thomas ran into the bathroom after playing outside. His face was red and wet. Little drops sat on his nose and forehead.

"Mommy, look!" Thomas said. "My face is leaking!"

Mommy put down the towel she was folding. She felt his forehead with her cool hand. "You ran so fast in the sun," she said. "Your skin let the water out to cool you down."

Thomas watched a drop dry in the mirror. Then his face felt cooler too. "The water dried and made me cool," he said.

Mommy turned on the tap. Warm water first, then cool. "Not too hot," she said. "Hot water can hurt your skin."

Thomas washed his hands with the rough washcloth. The water felt just right. "I almost forgot to wash behind my ears," he giggled.

Mommy dried his face softly. Thomas smiled at the boy in the mirror.

Miles went to the library with Mom. He saw a little fridge by the snack corner. The back of the fridge felt warm. "Is it broken?" Miles asked. "No," said the librarian. "The fridge keeps food cold by pulling heat out of the inside and pushing it out the back. That is why the back feels warm." Miles touched it again. Warm, but not broken.

Then the librarian hung a picture of a bus on the wall. She carried a heavy tablet to a little table. Miles pressed the big button. The screen turned on! He opened the drawing app. He drew a bus, round and yellow.

"All done?" Mom asked. "All done," said Miles. He pressed the button and put the tablet away. The drawing app slept. Miles waved bye to the warm little fridge.
